## Learning objectives

By the end of this opening, you should be able to state the research question,
identify the unit represented by a row of data, describe what another
researcher would need to retrace a result, and explain how Git and GitHub
record, review, and share changes.

You will read the workshop's Git history yourself, then watch the
environment, metadata, versioning, and archiving demonstrations. In the hands-on segment you will complete and run the pipeline
and revise its report. If you arrive late, finish
[preparation](00_preparation.qmd) during the demonstrations.

## Why this matters

Allow about three minutes. A reported result is easier to evaluate when its
data, analytical decisions, code, and software environment can be traced.
Sharing code helps, but the code also needs identifiable inputs and
instructions that work beyond its author's current R session.

In this workshop, **reproducibility** means being able to rerun a documented
workflow with its specified inputs and environment. **Open science** also
concerns how methods and outputs can be inspected, accessed, and reused.
Reproducibility does not establish that the scientific assumptions are correct,
and openness still needs to respect licences and access conditions.

Throughout the session, ask whether another researcher could understand,
rerun, audit, trace, reuse, and cite the work. The
[introduction](../1_introduction.qmd#intro-principles) lists
these principles.

## Our example: health and well-being

Allow about two minutes. The teaching question is: **What association between
health and well-being is reported across the included studies?** We use the
`HealthWellbeing` correlation example [@harrer2021, sec. 4.2.4].

Each row is a **study summary**, not a participant record. The columns are:

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `author` | Study label |
| `cor` | Reported Pearson correlation |
| `n` | Study sample size |
| `population` | Sample population description |
| `country` | Study country |

The [preparation activity](00_preparation.qmd#preparation-data) verifies the
snapshot. There is no need to fit a model during this opening.

Later, the pipeline pools correlations using Fisher's z transformation and an
explicit random-effects specification. Study independence, comparable effect
definitions, and differences between study populations need consideration.
A pooled association alone does not establish a causal effect.

## One workflow throughout the session

We follow this dataset through one connected workflow. The first half uses
short demonstrations; in the second half, you complete, run, and change the
analysis yourself.

| Time | Stage | Question we will answer | Tools | Format |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–10 min | Version the work | What changed, why, and who reviewed it? | Git, GitHub | Conceptual and hands-on |
| 10–20 min | Record the environment | Which software is needed? | renv, Docker, Binder | Demonstration |
| 20–28 min | Document the input | What can a collaborator learn about the data and how to reuse them? | dataspice, rfair | Demonstration |
| 28–35 min | Version data and models | Which input and model produced this result? | pins, vetiver | Demonstration |
| 35–50 min | Run the analysis | Which steps depend on this input? | targets | Hands-on |
| 50–65 min | Report the result | How are methods, results, and provenance connected? | Quarto | Hands-on |
| 65–75 min | Modify and reproduce | What rebuilds when an analysis setting changes, and does the result reproduce? | targets, Quarto | Hands-on |
| 75–82 min | Release and archive | How can this version be found and cited? | GitHub releases, Zenodo | Conceptual |
| 82–90 min | Questions and discussion | What would you change in your own work? | | Interactive |

The aim is to understand and experience the whole workflow, not to master each
package.

## Version control with Git and GitHub {#git-github}

Allow about four minutes. **Git** records the history of
a project's files. **GitHub** hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration
tools such as issues, pull requests, and releases.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Commit | A recorded change to one or more files, with a message explaining why |
| Branch | A line of work that can change without affecting the main version |
| Remote | A copy of the repository elsewhere, such as on GitHub |
| Push | Send local commits to a remote repository |
| Pull request | A proposal to merge a branch, with a place for review and discussion |
| Release | A named, tagged version of the repository, covered later in the session |

### Read the workshop's history {#git-history}

Allow about two minutes. The project in your MyBinder session is a copy
of the files without their Git history, but Git can read the history of
the public repository directly. Open the **Terminal** tab beside the
Console and run each block in the same Terminal. The commands only read
from GitHub and change nothing in your project.

1.  **Which versions have been released?** List the repository's tags
    without downloading anything else.

    ``` bash
    url=https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.git
    git ls-remote --tags --refs "$url"
    ```

    Each line pairs a commit hash with a version tag. A tag gives one
    commit a permanent name. The archiving segment shows how each
    tagged release is archived with its own DOI.

2.  **What changed recently, and why?** Copy the history into a
    temporary folder. `--filter=blob:none` fetches the commits and the
    lists of files they changed, but not the file contents, so it takes
    a few seconds.

    ``` bash
    git clone --quiet --bare --filter=blob:none "$url" /tmp/workshop-history.git
    git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git log --oneline --no-merges -5
    git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git log --oneline -3 -- pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R
    ```

    The first log lists the latest changes, and each message says what
    changed. The second lists only the commits that changed the
    reference pipeline you will run later.

3.  **Is your copy of the pipeline the latest version?** Git identifies
    each version of a file by a hash of its contents. Compare your copy
    with the one in the latest commit.

    ``` bash
    git hash-object pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R
    git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git rev-parse HEAD:pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R
    ```

    Matching lines mean identical contents. If they differ, the
    repository changed after your MyBinder image was built. This is why
    a result should cite a specific commit or release rather than "the
    latest version". The pipeline records checksums of its inputs for
    the same reason.

If you run the clone again, Git reports that the folder already exists;
your first copy is still there, so continue. If GitHub cannot be
reached, follow the instructor's screen.

The instructor then shows the same history on GitHub: a merged pull
request with its **Files changed** view, and the releases page, which
turns tags into named releases with notes.

The lockfile, exercise templates, and reference solutions are tracked.
Your edits in `workspace/` are personal working copies. Save them with
your report and provenance records using the
[export checklist](09_discussion.qmd#export-work). The raw teaching
snapshot and its licence notice are tracked too.

## Discuss with a neighbour

Allow about one minute. Name one thing you would ask for if a collaborator sent
only a pooled correlation. Choose from the data version, variable definitions,
analysis settings, code revision, or software environment, and explain why it
would matter.

## Checkpoint {#open-science-checkpoint}

You should be able to complete this sentence:

> To retrace this result, I need the source and version of the study summaries,
> the analysis decisions and code, and the environment used to run them.

You can also explain the difference between a local commit, a push to a
remote, and a pull request. You can say what the hash comparison told
you about your copy of the pipeline.

**Takeaway:** keep a traceable connection between the input, the decisions, and
the output. Next, we record the
[computational environment](02_environments.qmd).

## After the workshop: practise Git with your fork {#git-practice}

This optional exercise takes about ten minutes. It needs a GitHub account, a
fork of the
[workshop repository](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r)
cloned as your `origin`, and GitHub authentication in your environment. Run the
commands in the **Terminal** at the root of that clone.

1. Create a working branch:

   ```bash
   git switch -c workshop/health-wellbeing
   ```

2. Create `WORKSHOP_NOTES.md` in the project root as a provenance note.
   Replace the placeholders with your own information.

   ```markdown
   # Health and well-being: workshop notes

   Author: YOUR NAME

   ## Data source

   - Dataset: HealthWellbeing.
   - Book: Harrer, Cuijpers, Furukawa, and Ebert (2021), section 4.2.4.
   - Book URL: https://doing-meta.guide/pooling-es#correlations
   - Dataset documentation: https://dmetar.protectlab.org/reference/healthwellbeing
   - Download: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MathiasHarrer/dmetar/38c9b9bb5f85ea49de33e5d2536f6544d5268517/data/HealthWellbeing.rda
   - Retrieved: YYYY-MM-DD
   - Raw file: data/raw/healthwellbeing.rda
   - MD5: 0d74964b0b7168379a2b015cb648b326

   ## Decisions

   Preserve the raw file unchanged. Keep derived data and analysis outputs separate.
   Check upstream reuse terms before redistributing data.
   ```

3. Stage the note explicitly, inspect what will be committed, and commit it.
   Newly created files appear in `git diff --cached` after staging.

   ```bash
   git add WORKSHOP_NOTES.md
   git diff --cached -- WORKSHOP_NOTES.md
   git commit -m "docs(workshop): record HealthWellbeing data source"
   git log -1 --oneline
   ```

   If Git asks for an identity, configure your name and preferred commit email
   for this repository, then retry.

4. Push the branch to your fork and open a pull request **within your fork**,
   comparing the branch with its `main` branch:

   ```bash
   git push --set-upstream origin workshop/health-wellbeing
   ```

Ask a colleague to check that the data source is identifiable and the note
describes what you actually did. For a substantive contribution to the teaching
repository, follow its
[contribution guidance](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
and [AI assistance policy](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md).
A pull request provides a place for review; opening one does not mean that
human review is complete.
